extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and practitioners advising on equitable relief for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how courts should grant, refuse, or condition interlocutory and final injunctions to restrain patent infringement, including factors the court weighs and procedural prerequisites. Focuses on equitable discretion, proofs required, effects of delay, and procedural devices (sending to law, feigned issues, bonds, accounts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubt as to infringement requires jury trial/feigned issue
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question of infringement is doubtful, it must be tried by a jury; a feigned issue may be ordered only when the opinion of a jury is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court alone decides whether there is any doubt as to infringement and a feigned issue is not a matter of right — the applicant must lay a foundation for it. (Cases: Muntz; Van Hook v. Pendleton; remarks of Nelson, J. and Betts, J.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court determines whether doubt exists (not automatic jury)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is for the court alone to decide whether there is any doubt as to the matter of infringement; sending the question to a jury is discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where parties request a trial by jury or feigned issue, the chancellor/court must be brought to doubt on the question of identity before ordering one; after a jury verdict the court may still set it aside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on defendant’s business / irreparable mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction should not be granted where irreparable mischief would ensue to the defendant's business and the plaintiff would not be injured by delay or can be fully protected by interim accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies where granting the injunction would deprive the defendant of substantial lawful use of invested capital or throw employees out of work. The court balances prevention of mischief with preserving each party's benefit; if plaintiff can be fully protected (e.g., by keeping an account), injunction may still be refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunctions: discretionary multi-factor test
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding interlocutory (temporary) injunctions courts consider: the state of the litigation, where the plaintiff's title is denied; the nature of the improvement; the character and extent of the infringement complained of; and the comparative inconvenience to the parties by allowing or denying the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is latitude for discretion—orders may be granted or refused outright or upon terms/conditions. (Quoted from Judge Curtis in Forbush v. Bradford.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical operational effects matter (e.g., inability to alter machines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practical effect of an injunction on a defendant's operations (for example, inability to use entire machines without the patented improvement) is a relevant consideration in the injunction decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if alteration is possible, if in the present state of business no prudent man would alter, the injunction would effectively stop operations and weigh against granting unless plaintiff's right is firmly established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may impose conditions (bond, accounting, periodic filings)
rubrics_metrics.description: When granting an interlocutory injunction the court may impose terms such as requiring defendants to give bond, keep an account of quantities produced, file such accounts under oath periodically, and be liable for any final decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: order defendants within ten days to give bond with sufficient surety, keep account of cloth made on each loom, file such account under oath once in three months, and pay any final decree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's laches/delay or allowing defendant to incur expense can bar injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction will not be granted where the plaintiff permitted the defendant to proceed and incur expense under expectation of receiving a sum, if relations allow the defendant to dispute the patentee's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff has delayed unreasonably or allowed defendant to enter into contracts or investments, equity disfavors enjoining performance later. However, if defendant is estopped at law from denying patent validity, injunction may still be granted; if substantial sums (e.g., a year's rent) are due, the court may order money paid into court pending trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts made with implied understanding of damages only — no injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a defendant entered into a contract which was confessedly in violation of patentee's right but did so with implied understanding that disputes would be resolved as a matter of damages, an injunction should not restrain completion of the contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects parties who contracted under an expectation that liability would be handled as damages rather than injunctive relief (case: Smith v. Sharp Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of possession and actual infringement supports injunction despite promises
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff shows the necessary possession and an infringement has actually been committed by the defendant, an injunction will be granted notwithstanding the defendant's admission and promise not to repeat the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere promise by defendant not to repeat the infringement is insufficient to protect the plaintiff; the court may still interfere to prevent past acts from recurring (cases: Losh v. Hague; remarks of Sir L. Shadwell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuation without offering compensation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation that the infringement has been discontinued is not a sufficient answer to an injunction motion unless the defendant offers compensation for unlawful prior use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for compensation or other protective measures rather than naked assertions of discontinuance (case: Sickels v. Mitchell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final hearing differs: perpetual injunction generally only at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetual (final) injunctions are in general only granted at final hearing; objections to validity raised at hearing are treated differently because plaintiff had prior opportunities to seek interlocutory relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff could have (but did not) apply for interlocutory injunction earlier, the court may refuse final relief and even dismiss the bill with costs if suit has been pending a long time and answer denied validity and infringement (case: Bacon v. Jones; Lord Cottenham quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: When plaintiff must be sent to law to try title before injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff will be sent to try his title at law without a previous injunction if he does not show long possession and exercise of the exclusive right, where evidence casts doubt on originality or infringement, or where the patent contains gross and obvious defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed temporal standard; generally the time between patent grant and injunction application must be sufficient to show public repeated sales or construction under the claim. Prior recoveries/licenses that appear collusive will not suffice. (Cases and commentary cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use/recoveries/licenses count only if under same or legally connected patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Former use or recoveries relied upon as proof of possession must have been under the same patent or a patent legally connected with that under which the current application is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under systems allowing amended specifications or surrendering an old patent for a new one on account of informalities, rights may remain the same if the invention is the same; thus former possession under the old patent can ground an injunction under the amended patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant seeking issue out of chancery must plead prior use specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: If defendant wishes to have originality tried by an issue out of chancery, he must set out in his answer the names of places and persons where and by whom the invention had previously been used, as required by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural prerequisite because the act of Congress requires notice of those facts in a trial of originality at law (citation: Orr v. Merrill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of later patent by commissioner without interference notice is not a bar
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequent patentee cannot set up the commissioner's grant as a bar on infringement issues where the commissioner gave no notice of interference to the prior patentee; such grant is an ex parte opinion and not binding on the prior patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commissioner's action has quasi-judicial character but, absent interference notice, the prior patentee is not bound by the later grant (case: Wilson v. Barnum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions require the right to be sufficiently clear
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for a preliminary injunction should not be granted unless the right is clear in favor of the complainant; courts are not bound by a jury verdict where the evidence is very conflicting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will not routinely grant preliminary relief when the evidence is conflicting; the court must be satisfied of entitlement on the interlocutory record (case: Sickels v. Young).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long undisputed public possession may justify injunction until trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patentees have had reasonably long and undisputed possession against all the world, the court may grant an injunction until the legal question can be tried because less inconvenience may follow than dissolving it and risking public violation of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice (e.g., Boulton & Watt) shows courts sometimes favor injunctions on grounds of public allowance of possession; the injunction is interlocutory and does not decide final rights but preserves the patentee pending legal determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity's power vs convenience: sending to law to inform conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: The chancellor may order a trial at law to inform his conscience rather than because either party has a right to it; practice rests on convenience and the sound discretion of the court rather than absolute rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In U.S. practice, especially where complex mechanical or scientific questions are involved, courts may decide without sending to law, but often direct a law action when convenient for investigating legal titles and facts (Goodyear v. Day and commentary).
